subtype: Approach: talk to the bank about restructuring before missing a payment [Revision]
passage: Suraj's job offer was delayed by three months, and the first instalment of the education loan was due in five weeks. Sitting in the flat in Bengaluru with the loan papers, Suraj felt the old urge to wait and hope. Instead, the next morning, Suraj went to the bank branch before any payment was missed and asked for Disha, the officer who handled the account. "My start date has been pushed back. I don't want to default. What are my options?" Disha listened, checked the file, and explained that the tenure could be discussed and a new schedule drawn up in writing. Suraj brought the papers home and saw that the situation had turned from a dread into a task with a date.

qa.q: How many weeks until the first instalment was due?
qa.a: The first instalment was due in five weeks.

qa.q: What did Suraj feel before deciding to go to the bank?
qa.a: Suraj felt the urge to wait and hope, which suggests worry and a wish to avoid the problem.

qa.q: What could Suraj do while waiting for the job, and why?
qa.a: Suraj could set aside whatever small income arrives to be ready for the first payment, because preparing shows good faith.

qa.q: How might Disha see a customer who comes before missing a payment?
qa.a: Disha probably sees someone who takes the loan seriously, and finds it easier to work out options together.

grounding: When a job start is delayed a borrower meets the bank early, explains the situation and asks about options such as a longer tenure.

subtype: Approach: talk to the bank about restructuring before missing a payment [Revision]
passage:
'The company mailed again,' Santosh said at dinner. 'Joining is pushed to March now.'
Pankaj, his father, put the roti down. 'And the loan EMI starts in January.'
'I know. I was thinking I'd just borrow from Mama for two months and not tell the bank.'
'And if March becomes May?'
Santosh was quiet. 'Then I'd be stuck.'
'So who should know first?'
'The bank.' He rubbed his face. 'Tomorrow I'll go to the branch. Take the offer letter and the delay mail.'
'What will you ask?'
'Whether the start can move, or the tenure get longer so the EMI is smaller for a while. Whatever options they have.'
The next evening he was back. 'The manager said coming before a missed payment makes a real difference. They're reviewing a three-month extension of the moratorium. I have to send the documents by Friday.'
Pankaj nodded. 'Good. Send them Thursday.'

qa.q: When is Santosh's new joining date?
qa.a: Joining is pushed to March now.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when he went quiet?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and a little cornered, seeing that the quiet borrowing plan could leave him stuck.

qa.q: What else could Santosh bring or ask at the branch?
qa.a: Something in writing about his expected start date and salary, and questions about any charges for the extension, so he understands every option.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see his son's first idea?
qa.a: Pankaj sees a risky shortcut and, instead of lecturing, asks questions until Santosh chooses to go to the bank himself.

grounding: Shows a borrower whose job start is delayed going to the bank early to ask about options before any payment is missed.

subtype: Approach: talk to the bank about restructuring before missing a payment [Revision]
passage:
I'm Shalini. Last December my offer letter said I'd start on 2 January. Then HR sent a one-line mail: onboarding postponed, 'likely April'. My EMI of ₹8,200 was due from 15 January.
My first thought was to stay silent and scrape it together somehow. My cousin had done that. Then my friend Samir told me his elder brother had tried the same and ended up with late fees stacked three months deep.
That changed my mind. On 20 December, before any payment was due, I went to the branch with the offer letter and the postponement mail. I was shaking a little. The officer read both, asked about my savings, and explained two options: a short extra moratorium, or a longer tenure with a smaller EMI. I chose the moratorium till April.
The officer said most people come in after missing three payments. I came in before missing one.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel walking into the branch?
qa.a: Shalini was nervous, shaking a little, yet determined to act before any payment was missed.

qa.q: What would you advise someone choosing between the two options Shalini was offered?
qa.a: Ask the bank to show the total cost of each, and talk it over with a qualified adviser or trusted adult before signing.

qa.q: What would change if Shalini had stayed silent like the cousin?
qa.a: Missed EMIs could have piled up late fees, as happened to Samir's brother, and the bank would have seen a defaulter rather than someone acting in good faith.

grounding: Shows a borrower whose job start is postponed meeting the bank before a missed payment and choosing between the options offered.
